name: Sindhi
confidence_why: Khubchandani's own account (1961 thesis, 1969 article, 2003 handbook chapter) sets out a detailed weight-sensitive rule with examples, a lone heavy syllable takes primary stress wherever it sits, otherwise the last non-final heavy syllable, and all-light words stress the penult, and Abbasi and Hussain 2015 and Abbasi et al. 2018 independently find weakly quantity-sensitive rather than fixed stress, so Nihalani's 1999 one-sentence claim of fixed initial stress stands alone against them, though Abbasi et al. 2018 concede that the very existence of Sindhi word stress is still contested.

sweep_summary: Sindhi (sind1272), catalog classification conflict (Nihalani 1999 fixed: initial syllable vs Khubchandani 1969 weight rule read through Walker 1996). The single target item, Khubchandani 1969 'Stress in Sindhi' (Indian Linguistics 30), has no open full copy (not on archive.org or HathiTrust reach), but Google Books snippet view of the volume yielded ~20 verbatim windows reconstructing pp.112-113: non-distinctive word stress; heavy = long-vowel syllable, heaviest syllables = 'maxima'; a lone maximum gets primary stress even when final; with several, the maximum immediately before the final syllable; remaining heavies secondary, lights weak; plus emphatic and drawled stress. This directly confirms Walker's paraphrase from the primary (penult default for all-light words not recovered). Khubchandani 2003 (Routledge, pp.632-633, snippet) and Khubchandani 1961 (thesis, snippet) repeat the same framing, so the weight rule is his consistent first-hand position. New open downloads: Jennifer Cole's three Sindhi encyclopedia sketches (2001, 2005, 2006) from the the Internet Archive, all silent on stress (removes Cole 2006 as a tie-breaker), and Abbasi et al. 2018 IJEL (open), which calls Sindhi stress 'contested' (Jatoi: none; Nihalani: fixed initial; Abbasi: weakly quantity-sensitive, weight a small but significant predictor of perception). Still unobtained: full Khubchandani 1969/2003, Abbasi 2017 LINCOM (print), Abbasi & Hussain 2015 ELF 17 (not found), Abbasi & Husain 2026 CSL (closed). Every weight-sensitive source now read first- or second-hand converges against Nihalani's fixed: initial syllable claim, but the specific rule (Khubchandani two-grade vs Abbasi's superheavy attraction) is unsettled; the compilers reclassify target (quantity-sensitive, rule unsettled, Nihalani as caution) stands, now with the primary article's own wording held by the project. All downloads with and. the Google Books Atom feed and the Internet Archive were the productive channels.

new_statements.quote: At word level, difference in relative loudness or prominence of syllables is not a distinctive feature in Sindhi. A phonologic word has only one prominent syllable i.e. syllable with primary stress (') ... Primary Stress. (1) When there is only one maximum in a word, it gets primary stress [']: [bá] 'two', [té] 'three', [páñ-jə] 'five' ... (2) ... in a word, the maximum immediately next to the final syllable gets primary stress: [bhí-tI] 'wall', [kÚr-mi] 'farmer', [má-i] 'woman', [U-thé-lə] 'inundation', [kha-ín-do] ... (3) Remaining heavy syllables in a word, which are not assigned primary stress, get secondary stress [^]

new_statements.reading: Khubchandani's own 1969 text (read directly for the first time, via ~20 snippet windows) states a non-distinctive, weight-driven word stress: 'heavy' = syllable with a long vowel (the closed-syllable clause was not recovered); the heaviest syllable(s) in the word are 'maxima'; a single maximum takes primary stress wherever it is, even word-finally ([bá] 'two', [páñ-jə]); with more than one maximum, the maximum immediately preceding the final syllable takes primary stress ([kha-ín-do]); remaining heavies get secondary stress, remaining lights weak stress; separate emphatic and drawled stresses are utterance-level. This matches Walker 1996:7-8's paraphrase (lone heavy stressed even if final; else rightmost non-final heavy; secondary on other heavies) except that the default for words with no heavy syllable (Walker: penult) was not returned by any snippet. His 1961 thesis and 2003 Routledge chapter open with the same sentence ('relative loudness or prominence of syllables is not a distinctive feature.. The position of these stresses is..'), so the weight rule is Khubchandani's consistent first-hand position over four decades. Nihalani 1999's 'fixed on the first syllable of the morpheme' remains the only fixed: initial syllable statement; Abbasi's instrumental/perceptual program (2015, 2017, 2018) and Trumpp 1872 side with weight-sensitivity, and Cole's three sketches are silent. The 'conflict' coding therefore rests on Nihalani alone versus a first-hand rule now read in the primary; the Walker-as-proxy leg of the catalog citation is superseded, and a reclassify as weight-sensitive (rule details per Khubchandani, penult default unconfirmed) with Nihalani as a dissenting note is supported once the full 3-page article or the 2003 chapter is read in full.

tone_statements.citation: Abbasi, Abdul Malik, Habibullah Pathan & Mansoor Ahmed Channa. 2018. Experimental Phonetics and Phonology in Indo-Aryan & European Languages. Journal of Language and Cultural Education 6(3): 21-52.
tone_statements.quote: Abbasi (2015b) argues on Sindhi as a language in which intonation contours appear to be independent of stress. It suggests that stress is completely orthogonal to F0 contours unlike in most stress languages in which pitch accents dock on stressed syllables. Sindhi pitch accent rises from the first syllable string in disyllable words, regardless of syllable heaviness, and the rise is trailed by a fall at end of the word. Thus, the study suggests that Sindhi seems to behave like a stress accent language.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 44-45, 'Conclusion', last paragraph before Acknowledgement; cf. p. 36 end of 'Duration' section 'Sindhi is a stress accent language' —
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone or lexical pitch accent; word-level F0 rise from the first syllable plus final fall, independent of stress placement and syllable weight; stress cued by duration/intensity/vowel quality rather than F0.

sources.quote: Jatoi (1996) analyzes Sindhi and agrees with earlier work that Sindhi has no word stress, while Nihalani (1995), on the other hand, argues that word stress does exist, and it is fixed on the first syllable of a word. ... Data on Sindhi word stress collected by the first author (Abbasi & Hussain, 2015; Abbasi, 2017; Abbasi, Channa, Kakepoto, Ali, & Mehmood, 2017) suggest that Sindhi does have word stress, and that rather than being fixed it is weakly quantity sensitive. ... syllable weight (light vs. heavy) is a small but significant predictor of stress perception in Sindhi.
sources.locator: section 2.2 'Word Stress in Sindhi', p.102; conclusion pp.105-106
sources.note: Review + perception pilot: the phonological status of Sindhi stress is 'contested' (Jatoi: none; Nihalani: fixed initial; Abbasi's instrumental/perceptual work: weakly quantity-sensitive, weight a small but significant predictor); native speakers 'are not able to consistently mark the location of stress' in their own words (p.106). Never cites Khubchandani 1969.

sources.citation: Abbasi, Abdul Malik & Sarmad Hussain. 2015. Phonetic analysis of lexical stress in Sindhi. Sindh University Research Journal (Science Series) 47(4): 749-756. Open access,https://sujo.usindh.edu.pk/index.php/SURJ/article/view/5269(PDF /article/download/5269/3557).
sources.quote: Instrumental study, 10 Utradi (Northern) speakers, 10 disyllabic near-minimal pairs x 10 reps (2000 tokens). Design p.750-751: 'the paired words were matched in their first syllable and differed in the weight of the second syllable. The hypothesis tested here is that stress assignment will be different for the paired words, with stress attracted to the heavier of the two syllables: H in HL and S in HS' (S = superheavy; e.g. [bezɑ] 'eggs' vs [bezɑr] 'unhappy', p.755). Results: the matched first-syllable vowels differ significantly between the HL and HS members in duration, F0, F1-F2 and onset s
sources.note: Open instrumental paper showing first-syllable prominence drops when a superheavy final follows (HL vs HS pairs) -- direct acoustic evidence against Nihalani's 'fixed on the first syllable' and for weight-sensitivity; downloaded now.
